---
title: "Milestones"
subtitle: "Twelve things you will have built by 6 August 2027. Each one is something you would be willing to put in front of a researcher who does this for a living."
toc-depth: 2
---

Days pass and leave nothing behind unless you write something down. These twelve are what the year is
actually for; the other three hundred and fifty-three days feed them.

Each milestone replaces that week's catch-up day. The work happens during the week. The milestone day is
where it becomes a document — which means if the week went badly, the milestone tells you so, and that
is the point.

A note on what "good" means here. Every milestone below has a **How you know it's good** line, and in
almost every case it is a line about honesty rather than performance. A milestone that reports a Sharpe
of 3.1 and cannot say how many strategies were tried before that one is a worse artifact than one
reporting 0.6 with a confidence interval. Interviewers at the firms you are targeting can tell the
difference in about ninety seconds, and so can you.

---

## Milestone 1 — Market map and a point-in-time data store {#m28}

**[Day 28](days/day-028.qmd), Thursday 3 September 2026.** Fed by weeks 1–4.

Two things: a written map of the industry, and working code that stores prices without lying about
what was knowable when.

**What's in it**

- A one-page map of who pays whom: exchanges, brokers, clearing, market makers, prop shops, pod shops,
  long-only managers, allocators. For each, where the revenue comes from. This exists so that eleven
  months from now you can tell which firm you are actually interviewing at.
- A glossary in your own words of every instrument you met — share, ETF, future, option, bond, forward —
  written as "what this contract obliges each side to do", not as a definition you copied.
- A DuckDB or Parquet store of daily bars for a universe you chose and can defend, with splits and
  dividends handled explicitly, and a documented answer to "what did this series look like on 12 March
  2019, using only information available on 12 March 2019".
- The ingestion re-runs from scratch with one command.

**How you know it's good** — you can state what your data source does *not* contain (delisted names?
restated fundamentals? the actual close or the auction print?) without going to look.

---

## Milestone 2 — Stylized facts and the noise floor {#m63}

**[Day 63](days/day-063.qmd), Thursday 8 October 2026.** Fed by weeks 5–9.

The document you will reread every time a backtest looks good. Half empirical, half simulation.

**What's in it**

- The stylized facts, measured on your own data rather than quoted: the return distribution against a
  fitted normal, an estimated tail index, the autocorrelation of returns next to the autocorrelation of
  absolute returns, and the leverage effect.
- The Sharpe ratio treated as an estimator. Its standard error at your sample length. What serial
  correlation does to it. How long a track record has to be before a Sharpe of 1 is distinguishable from
  0 at any confidence you would act on.
- **The noise floor**: a simulation that answers, for your own research process, how high a backtested
  Sharpe must be before it is evidence of anything, given the number of specifications you will try.
  Deflated Sharpe, and the probability of backtest overfitting, computed rather than cited.
- One paragraph mapping each of the above onto the equivalent problem in genome-wide association
  studies, because that mapping is the thing you will say in an interview that nobody else says.

**How you know it's good** — it produces a specific number that you are willing to be held to for the
rest of the year, and you actually apply it in milestone 3.

---

## Milestone 3 — A pairs strategy that survives out of sample {#m98}

**[Day 98](days/day-098.qmd), Thursday 12 November 2026.** Fed by weeks 10–14.

The first end-to-end strategy. Deliberately the most-published, most-degraded idea in the field, so that
the exercise is about method rather than about finding an edge.

**What's in it**

- The pair selection procedure, stated *before* the results, including how many pairs were screened.
  That count feeds directly into milestone 2's correction.
- Cointegration tested properly — Engle-Granger and Johansen, with the difference explained — plus the
  estimated half-life of mean reversion and the trading rule derived from it rather than tuned onto it.
- A hedge ratio that is allowed to move, via the Kalman filter from week 14, compared against a static one.
- Out-of-sample results on a period you did not look at while developing, with costs, and the same
  procedure run on synthetic independent random walks to show the false-positive rate of your own pipeline.

**How you know it's good** — you can say what would have made you abandon it, and whether that condition
was met. If the honest answer is "it doesn't work after costs", the milestone is complete and successful.

## Milestone 4 — A factor risk model built from scratch {#m133}

**[Day 133](days/day-133.qmd), Thursday 17 December 2026.** Fed by weeks 15–19.

Not a call to a library. The covariance matrix, the factor exposures, and the decomposition, built by you.

**What's in it**

- A covariance matrix over a few hundred names, estimated three ways — sample, Ledoit-Wolf shrunk, and
  factor-based — with the eigenvalue spectrum plotted against the Marchenko-Pastur bound so it is visible
  which eigenvalues carry information.
- Factor exposures for market, size, value and momentum, and a decomposition of one portfolio's risk into
  factor and idiosyncratic parts.
- The same portfolio optimized under each covariance estimate, and the out-of-sample realized risk of
  each, against equal weighting as the benchmark.
- A position-sizing section: what full Kelly implies, what fraction of it you would actually run, and the
  drawdown you are accepting by choosing that fraction.

**How you know it's good** — equal weighting appears in the comparison and is not quietly excluded when
it wins.

---

## Milestone 5 — The research platform {#m161}

**[Day 161](days/day-161.qmd), Thursday 14 January 2027.** Fed by weeks 20–23.

The single most valuable artifact of the year, and the one an interviewer will ask the most questions
about. Everything after this is built on it.

**What's in it**

- An event-driven backtester that consumes point-in-time data, applies a documented cost model, and
  produces a standard result object.
- A transaction cost model with the components separated — spread, impact, borrow, financing — and a
  chart of net Sharpe against turnover, so the strategy's sensitivity to costs is visible rather than
  assumed.
- **A test suite whose job is to make look-ahead impossible rather than unlikely.** At minimum: a test
  that feeds the engine data with future values deliberately poisoned and asserts the results are
  unchanged; a test on synthetic data with an analytically known answer; and a null-strategy test whose
  distribution of outcomes you have characterised.
- A written list of every lie your backtester still tells, ranked by how much it matters. There will be
  several. This list is the most impressive part of the document.

**How you know it's good** — someone else could clone it, run one command, and reproduce a result you
report elsewhere in the year.

---

## Milestone 6 — The alpha book {#m203}

**[Day 203](days/day-203.qmd), Thursday 25 February 2027.** Fed by weeks 24–29.

Five to eight signals, each characterised the way a research desk characterises one.

**What's in it**

- Per signal: the economic reason it might work stated *first*, then information coefficient and its
  decay profile, information ratio, quantile spread, turnover, and estimated capacity in dollars.
- The correlation matrix of the signals, and the combination — with the argument for why you combined
  the way you did rather than the way that scored best.
- At least one signal that does not work, kept in the book with the diagnosis.
- Everything run through the milestone-5 platform, with the multiple-testing correction from milestone 2
  applied to the whole set rather than to each signal in isolation.

**How you know it's good** — the number of specifications you tried is stated on the first page.

---

## Milestone 7 — Machine learning against the linear baseline {#m238}

**[Day 238](days/day-238.qmd), Thursday 1 April 2027.** Fed by weeks 30–34.

The report that decides whether the machine learning earned its complexity. Given your background this
is the milestone you are most at risk of doing well and concluding too much from.

**What's in it**

- The labelling scheme and why — fixed horizon against triple barrier — and the sample weights that
  overlapping outcomes force on you.
- Purged, embargoed cross-validation, with the embargo length justified from the autocorrelation of the
  labels rather than picked.
- A regularized linear model as the baseline, taken seriously and tuned as carefully as the gradient
  boosting. Most published comparisons lose here by not trying.
- The verdict on the same test set with the same costs, plus a permutation-importance analysis and an
  honest note on which features are proxies for something you did not intend.

**How you know it's good** — the conclusion is a number with an interval, and you would report it the
same way if it had come out the other direction.

---

## Milestone 8 — An option pricer and a delta-hedging study {#m280}

**[Day 280](days/day-280.qmd), Thursday 13 May 2027.** Fed by weeks 35–40.

Two artifacts: code that prices, and a simulation that shows what hedging actually earns.

**What's in it**

- A pricer implementing Black-Scholes analytically, a binomial tree, and Monte Carlo with at least one
  variance-reduction technique — all three agreeing to a stated tolerance, with the convergence of the
  last two plotted against the first.
- The greeks, computed analytically and by finite difference, agreeing.
- **The delta-hedging study**: simulate hedging a short option at some volatility while the underlying
  realizes another, and decompose the profit and loss. Show that the expected result is the gap between
  implied and realized variance, and show what discrete rebalancing costs you.
- A page on the variance risk premium: what it is, what the historical evidence says about its size, and
  why it is not free money.

**How you know it's good** — you can derive Black-Scholes on a whiteboard by the replication argument,
without notes, in ten minutes. Test yourself on this rather than assuming.

---

## Milestone 9 — Execution, impact and honest capacity {#m308}

**[Day 308](days/day-308.qmd), Thursday 10 June 2027.** Fed by weeks 41–44.

The milestone that revises every earlier number downward. Expect that and report it plainly.

**What's in it**

- An impact model fitted to real intraday or order-book data, with the square-root form tested rather
  than assumed, and the fitted coefficient stated with its uncertainty.
- Your own slippage, measured against arrival price on the paper account, split into spread, impact and
  timing.
- The revised capacity of the milestone-6 alpha book once that impact model replaces the flat cost
  assumption, at several assumed asset levels.
- One paragraph on which of your strategies dies first as size grows, and why.

**How you know it's good** — it contains at least one earlier result that you now believe was wrong, said
in those words.

---

## Milestone 10 — The system in production {#m329}

**[Day 329](days/day-329.qmd), Thursday 1 July 2027.** Fed by weeks 45–47.

The strategy running by itself, against a real broker's paper account, without you.

**What's in it**

- Scheduled execution: data pull, signal computation, portfolio construction, order generation, submission,
  and reconciliation, each logged and each able to fail loudly.
- Monitoring that catches the failures that matter — stale data, a position that does not match the
  intended one, a fill far from the expected price, a signal outside its historical range.
- The reconciliation report: intended portfolio against actual portfolio, daily, with the difference
  explained.
- A runbook for the four or five things that will go wrong, written before they do.

**How you know it's good** — it survives a week where you do not touch it, and the log tells you what
happened without you having to reconstruct it.

---

## Milestone 11 — The interview dossier {#m357}

**[Day 357](days/day-357.qmd), Thursday 29 July 2027.** Fed by weeks 48–51 and by fifty drill sittings.

Everything a hiring process needs from you, assembled and rehearsed.

**What's in it**

- A CV rewritten for this industry, where the genetics work is described in the language of the job you
  want — instrumental variables, multiple testing, high-dimensional inference — without overclaiming or
  disowning it.
- Two-page write-ups of milestones 5, 6 and 8, each readable by someone with ten minutes.
- The problem log from the drill thread: what you have solved, what you got wrong, and the classes of
  problem you are still slow on.
- The five-minute research presentation, rehearsed against a clock and recorded once so you have heard it.
- The firm list with a reason next to each name, and the outreach actually sent.

**How you know it's good** — you can answer "why are you leaving academia" in three sentences that a
researcher at the firm would find convincing rather than polite.

## Milestone 12 — Capstone {#m365}

**[Day 365](days/day-365.qmd), Friday 6 August 2027.**

Three things.

**The research dossier** pulls the year into one document: the platform, the alpha book, the risk model,
the execution study, and the recommendation you would give a portfolio manager about which of it is worth
running and at what size.

**The track record** is whatever the paper account did, reported without adjustment. Months where it lost
money are in the table. If the live period disagrees with the backtest, that disagreement is the most
interesting result you have and it goes at the front.

**The retrospective** is the page you will value most in 2029: what you believed in September 2026 that
turned out to be wrong, what took three times longer than planned, which milestone you would drop, and
what you would do differently with the next 365 hours. Answer the [self-check](assessment.qmd) out loud
first — anything you cannot answer is not a failure, it is the reading list for the autumn.
